newsitem.title: USA: Cuban exiles mark anniversary of planes shootdown.
newsitem.headline: Cuban exiles mark anniversary of planes shootdown.

text.p: Cuban Americans dropped flowers in the sea off Cuba on Monday to remember four fliers from a Miami-based exile group who were killed when Cuban MiGs shot down their planes a year ago.
In what the exile community declared a "Day of Sorrow and Hope," friends and families mourned the dead and roundly denounced Cuban President Fidel Castro as a killer.
More than a dozen planes flew from Miami to the site in international waters north of Havana where the two Cessnas of the Brothers to the Rescue were downed on Feb. 24, 1996.
Warned by both Washington and Havana not to provoke another incident, they tossed wreaths and flowers into the waters of the Florida Straits and then returned without incident to Miami.

"We were actually over the graveyard where they are buried," Brothers founder Jose Basulto said on his return. "We said to them, 'we have not forgotten you. You are still our brothers. We will not let you down.'"

At a ceremony at Miami's Liberty Monument, people fell silent for seven minutes at 3:21 p.m. EST, the time the rocket attack began last year. They listened to a taped tribute to the fliers, including snatches of one pilot's final words.
"I hope they will always be remembered and I hope that some good will come out of this," Mirta Mendez, sister of victim Carlos Costa, told those present.
"We want to see Castro and the Cuban pilots brought to justice. We have to realize that Castro is the one that killed them. The truth is that they were murdered in cold-blood."
The attack shocked Miami's huge and predominantly anti-Castro Cuban American community and also had widespread international ramifications.

It raised tensions between Washington and Havana after a relative softening. It also forced President Bill Clinton to sign the Helms-Burton Act tightening the U.S. embargo on Cuba, which in turn dragged Washington into a trade dispute with Europe, Canada and Mexico.

Several hundred people, many waving Cuban flags, attended a memorial service at a monument to the four dead fliers outside the Brothers to the Rescue hangar before the planes took off to lay the wreaths.

Sylvia Iriondo, who was on a third plane flown by Basulto that returned safely that day, told mourners: "We cry for those who have died in the struggle for Cuba's freedom in defense of the rights of the Cuban people, especially for the ones who have been executed, imprisoned, assassinated, tortured, murdered, harassed and oppressed."

Basulto's organization searches the seas for refugees fleeing the Communist-ruled island, but one month before the shoot-down he had dropped anti-Castro leaflets over Havana. He flew off for Monday's ceremony in a co-pilot's seat as U.S. authorities have revoked his pilot's license.

A U.S. Coast Guard cutter was stationed at the site of the incident and other Coast Guard vessels made routine patrols in the area. Cuba, which has always said the attack was a legitimate act of self-defense, reinforced its marine patrols.
In Washington, Clinton honored the four victims and called for a transition to democracy in Cuba.

"The shoot-down and the Cuban government's continuing repression of human rights activists and independent journalists underscore the need to continue working for a peaceful transition to democracy in Cuba," he said.
In Little Havana, the heart of Cuban-American Miami, the anniversary was the topic of conversation on the sidewalks, call-in radio shows and at coffee bars.
Some questioned why the United States, whose military radar systems had detected the MiGs, did not act.
"They did nothing because they didn't want to have a problem with Cuba," said 67-year-old Miguel Romero.
In Havana, the names of the four dead exiles were read out during a mass on Monday morning at one Havana church, apparently put on a list of people to be mourned by relatives.

Cuban authorities reiterated the incident could have been prevented by the United States. Havana said at the time its patience was running out after numerous violations of its air space in the past 20 months.
